text_blocks.snippet: In New Hampshire, a DWI (Driving While Intoxicated) conviction stays on your criminal record for 10 years. However, after those 10 years, you can petition the court for an annulment, which will effectively seal the record from public access. The demerit points on your driving record from a DWI conviction, though, will remain for 3 years, according to NewHampshireCourtRecords.us.

related_questions.question: Is NH a zero tolerance state?
related_questions.snippet: If you're caught with even the smallest amount of alcohol in your system, it can turn your whole life upside down. That's because New Hampshire follows what's called a zero tolerance law. That means if you're under 21 and have a blood alcohol content (BAC) of 0.02% or higher, you're considered over the legal limit.

text_blocks.snippet: In New Hampshire, a DWI (Driving While Intoxicated), also known as DUI (Driving Under the Influence), is a serious offense. It's defined as driving or attempting to drive under the influence of alcohol or drugs, or with a blood alcohol content (BAC) of .08% or higher for adults, .02% or higher for those under 21, and .04% or higher for commercial drivers. Penalties for a first offense can include fines, license suspension, and mandatory programs like the Impaired Driver Intervention Program (IDIP). Aggravated DWI charges, which involve a higher BAC or other aggravating factors, carry even harsher penalties, including jail time.

text_blocks.snippet: Key Aspects of New Hampshire DWI Laws:

list.title: BAC Limits:
list.snippet: The legal limit for adults is .08% BAC, while those under 21 face a .02% limit, according to dui.drivinglaws.org.

list.title: "Under the Influence" Defined:
list.snippet: You can be charged with DWI even if your BAC is below the legal limit if law enforcement believes your ability to drive is impaired by alcohol or drugs, according to Russman Law.

list.title: First Offense:
list.snippet: Typically a class B misdemeanor, with potential for it to be a class A misdemeanor with aggravating factors.

list.title: Penalties for First Offense:
list.snippet: Fines (minimum of $500), license suspension (minimum of 9 months), and mandatory participation in an impaired driver education program (IDEP) and/or an Impaired Driver Care Management Program (IDCMP), according to NewHampshireCourtRecords.us.

list.title: Aggravated DWI:
list.snippet: Charges can be brought if the BAC is .16% or higher, or if other factors like speeding, driving with a minor, or eluding police are present.

list.title: Penalties for Aggravated DWI:
list.snippet: More severe penalties, including jail time (a minimum of 17 days, with some time possibly suspended), fines (minimum $750), and longer license suspensions.

list.title: Subsequent Offenses:
list.snippet: Penalties escalate with each subsequent DWI conviction, and can include felony charges and mandatory jail time.

list.title: Administrative License Suspension:
list.snippet: In addition to court-imposed penalties, a DWI arrest can trigger an administrative license suspension.

list.title: Impact on Insurance:
list.snippet: A DWI conviction will significantly increase your car insurance rates, according to Insurance.com.

list.title: Defenses:
list.snippet: It's crucial to understand that you have legal rights and potential defenses against a DWI charge, such as challenging the validity of the traffic stop, the accuracy of breathalyzer or other tests, or the field sobriety tests.

list.title: Importance of Legal Counsel:
list.snippet: If you are facing DWI charges, it's highly recommended to consult with an experienced New Hampshire DWI attorney.
